entry.title: Introducing Full Transaction Detection for Cloudflare WAF
entry.content:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough

Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OKContent-Type: text/plain[database]username=app_servicepassword=EXAMPLE_SECRET

Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.*  fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAFhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/full-transaction-waf/

entry.title: Cloudflare Deploys Protections Against Php2shell Vulnerability
entry.content:
Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.

All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule.

The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.

More information to follow.

October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.

Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.

Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.

Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.

To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.

Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog.

The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

What we know about the vulnerabilities

PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.

The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.

The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:

Vulnerability

What goes wrong

CVE-2026-109618

PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

CVE-2026-109619

A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.

Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.

New rules

For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior, you can refer to our documentation.

Rule Description

To better identify exploit attempts, Cloudflare developed full transaction detection, a new WAF capability that analyzes both sides of the same HTTP transaction. While some malicious payloads can be identified using the request alone, the response contains useful signals that can be used to create rules with higher confidence, reducing false positives. A matching full transaction rule can block the origin response before it reaches the requester. Learn how it works in our full transaction detection blog post.

The new Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default has been automatically deployed for customers on all plans, including Free. To verify that the response rules are active, you can visit the Security > Security Rules page. Read the full transaction blog to learn how to customize its deployment.

Review events and customize protection

To analyze blocked requests, visit Security > Security Analytics > Events. Filter by the rule IDs in the table above and inspect the matched request, action, and path. Events identify whether the action came from a managed or custom rule. Customers who need to tailor the protection can update the scope of the Managed Ruleset to the parts of an application where it is relevant.

Update PHP and keep the protection enabled

Cloudflare customers using our Managed Ruleset are protected by default. We recommend following the advisory recommendation and applying the vendor update to your PHP repos as soon as possible while keeping the WAF protection enabled as an additional protection. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge.

Copy prompt to fix!
# Security task: check and fix "php2shell" (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
Two critical PHP runtime vulnerabilities were disclosed on 2026-10-21 (CVSS v4.0 9.2).
They allow unauthenticated remote code execution, data exposure and DoS through crafted
HTTP requests. Exploitation is already happening. The bug is in the PHP runtime itself,
so updating app code, frameworks, WordPress or plugins does NOT fix it.
Official advisory (treat as source of truth, re-fetch it in case it was updated):
https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5
  • GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption)
  • GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state)
Fixed upstream versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35
Affected: every PHP install that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php,
php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed). mod_php has the highest risk: a demonstrated exploit
triggers before any application code runs.
Rules
  • Do NOT guess. If you can’t confirm a version or setting, say so.
  • Ask me before changing anything on production or shared infrastructure,
    restarting production services, or editing deploy config. Read-only discovery is fine.
  • Don’t stop at the first finding. Inventory everything, then report.
Step 1: Inventory every place PHP runs
Search the current repo/workspace AND any machines/containers I have access to:
  • Repo: *.php, composer.json/composer.lock (check require.php and
    config.platform.php), Dockerfile*, docker-compose*, .php-version,
    .tool-versions, .devcontainer/, CI files (GitHub Actions setup-php, GitLab CI
    image:), IaC (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, k8s manifests), PaaS config
    (app.yaml, Procfile, Platform.sh, Laravel Forge/Vapor, etc.).
  • Base images: list every FROM php:*, FROM wordpress:*, FROM bitnami/*,
    FROM serversideup/*, FROM dunglas/frankenphp* and similar, with tags.
  • Running hosts/containers (if accessible): php -v, php-fpm -v, php -i | grep -i "server api",
    apachectl -M | grep -i php, docker ps + docker exec <c> php -v.
  • Note the SAPI for each (FPM / mod_php / CGI / FrankenPHP / LiteSpeed / CLI-only).
  • Note long-running workers (Laravel Octane, RoadRunner, Swoole, FrankenPHP worker
    mode). These are relevant to the stale-state bug.
If no PHP is found anywhere, tell me clearly and stop. Nothing else is needed.
Step 2: Decide if each instance is vulnerable
For each instance, classify it as PATCHED / VULNERABLE / UNKNOWN:
  • Upstream builds: vulnerable if below 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 on that branch.
  • PHP 8.1 and older are EOL upstream: vulnerable unless a vendor backport is confirmed.
  • Distro packages (Debian/Ubuntu/RHEL/Alpine/etc.) often backport fixes WITHOUT
    bumping the upstream version, so php -v alone isn’t enough. Check the package
    changelog for the CVE IDs, e.g.
    apt changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]" or
    rpm -q --changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]".
  • If PHP comes from rpms.remirepo.net: the advisory says it will not have same-day
    updates. Flag this and recommend distro packages or building from source.
  • Managed hosting / shared hosting / PaaS: mark UNKNOWN and tell me to ask the provider.
Step 3: Fix (only after I approve the plan for prod)
  1. Upgrade PHP to a fixed version (or the vendor-patched package):
    • Bump Docker base image tags to a fixed patch release, rebuild, redeploy.
    • Update CI php-version pins.
    • apt/dnf/apk upgrade of the distro PHP packages.
    • 7.4 / 8.0 / 8.1 built from source: the PHP security team published minimal
      backport branches linked from the advisory. Otherwise upgrade to a supported version.
  2. Restart EVERY PHP worker (FPM pools, Apache, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Octane/
    RoadRunner/Swoole). Old processes keep running vulnerable code until restarted.
  3. Verify each instance afterwards (version + changelog check) and report the evidence.
Step 4: Temporary mitigations (ONLY if patching isn’t possible right away)
These reduce exposure but do NOT make the server safe. Apply them in php.ini / the FPM
pool / server config (not ini_set() or .user.ini) and restart every worker:
  • CVE-2026-109618:
    • memory_limit=-1, set non-overridably (e.g. php_admin_value), and confirm nothing
      re-applies a finite limit.
    • Low post_max_size (8M with no uploads, 32M with uploads), with
      upload_max_filesize below it.
    • Enforce request size / field count / multipart part count / header limits at the
      web server or proxy, including requests without Content-Length.
    • Use container/cgroup memory limits. Do NOT use RLIMIT_AS/RLIMIT_DATA.
  • CVE-2026-109619:
    • session.upload_progress.enabled=0.
    • On PHP 8.5: fatal_error_backtraces=0.
    • Remove invalid/deprecated per-request settings that emit diagnostics early (hiding
      them via error_reporting/display_errors/@ does not help).
    • Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts.
  • If the site sits behind Cloudflare: confirm the WAF Managed Ruleset is deployed in
    block mode (Free plans get the Managed Free Ruleset automatically). This is
    defense in depth, not a replacement for patching.
Step 5: Look for signs of compromise (read-only)
Since exploitation started before disclosure, check what you can access:
  • PHP-FPM/Apache error logs for segfaults, “Allowed memory size exhausted”, or
    worker crashes, especially clustered around unusually large POST/multipart requests.
  • Recently modified or unexpected files in web roots (webshells), new cron jobs,
    unexpected processes or outbound connections from PHP users.
    Report anything suspicious. Do not delete evidence.
Final report
Give me a table: location | how PHP is provided | SAPI | version | status
(PATCHED/VULNERABLE/UNKNOWN) | action taken or needed. Then list:
  • What you changed (files, commands), what still needs my approval, and anything that
    needs a hosting provider.
  • Mitigations applied as stopgaps and when they should be removed.
  • Any compromise indicators found.
Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerabilityhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/php-vulnerabilities-waf-protection/

entry.title: How Commerce.com and Cloudflare Are Getting Storefronts Ready for AI Agents
entry.content:
AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online.

That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it.

Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf.

In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code.

Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once?

Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way.

Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP

Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts:

“Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship.
We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly.
WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP, and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.”

Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic.

What a shopper's agent sees

When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP.

Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart."

Without WebMCP: The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers.

With WebMCP: The agent detects the store's tools on document.modelContext and makes two clean calls:

  1. search_products({ query: "trail running shoe", max_price: 140, size: 10 })
  2. add_to_cart({ product_id: "shoe_123" })

Because the agent runs inside your active browser session on the store's domain, your cart updates in real time. Commerce.com’s backend MCP server determines the commerce flow: when you’re ready to complete the purchase, you click checkout yourself — keeping your payment details secure and leaving you in complete control of the final buy.

What we built together

When Commerce.com asked to turn on WebMCP across almost 100000 storefronts, we ran into a practical challenge: WebMCP was originally designed as a single on-or-off switch for an entire domain zone.

Commerce wanted to enable our mcp-server-client toolpack, which acts as an edge bridge — proxying tool definitions and requests directly from Commerce.com’s backend MCP server to the visitor's browser. Because Commerce.com uses Cloudflare for SaaS to host thousands of merchant vanity domains on shared zones, we needed a way to deliver this platform-wide while giving individual store owners an easy way to opt out.

1. On for all stores on Commerce.com, with an opt-out for each merchant

Instead of building a complex custom allowlist, we hooked WebMCP into the existing Cloudflare concepts of Configuration Rules and custom hostname metadata.

Commerce.com turns WebMCP on for their main zone, then adds a rule at the edge that checks merchant metadata. If a merchant flips the "opt-out" switch in their Commerce.com dashboard, Cloudflare bypasses WebMCP for that specific storefront automatically:

{  "action": "set_config",  "expression": "cf.hostname.metadata.webmcp_opt_out eq \"true\"",  "action_parameters": {    "webmcp_enabled": false  }}

Because Cloudflare evaluates these rules at the edge before serving the page, an opted-out store gets zero extra latency, no remote lookups, and no injected scripts.

2. Tailored endpoints and safe fallbacks

As with any preview release, working with a partner in the real world revealed a few practical details we hadn't accounted for:

Custom MCP paths: When the mcp-server-client toolpack was enabled, our bridge originally expected to find every site's MCP server at /mcp. Commerce.com’s server lives at /api/mcp. To handle this, we added a configurable MCP URL setting at the zone level. When this is set, we pass the custom path into the injected script tag:

<script type="module"    src="https://cors.mhuig.top/?r=https://blog.cloudflare.com&url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/.webmcp/bridge.js"    data-packs="c2pa,mcp-server-client"    data-mcp-url="https://cors.mhuig.top/?r=https://blog.cloudflare.com&url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/api/mcp"></script>

Seamless fallbacks: If a store's MCP server is offline or a customer's browser doesn't support WebMCP, the script exits. The storefront loads normally and human shoppers aren't affected.

What's next

We'll keep investing in WebMCP as the standard evolves, starting with helping agents find a site's tools more easily. Cloudflare and Commerce.com will continue to work together to make shopping with agents fast, reliable and safe for both merchants and shoppers.

If you're at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco on October 21, 2026, come see us at Getting your storefront agent ready for peak season, a panel discussion featuring Kristina Pototska (Product Management Director, Commerce), Justis Blasco (CTO and Co-Founder, Popmenu), Ross Harvey (Head of Infrastructure, Fruugo), and Josh Mills (VP of Engineering, Gopuff).

How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agentshttps://blog.cloudflare.com/webmcp-commerce/

entry.title: 解道题奖金100万元！华为第七届奥林帕斯奖启动全球征集：聚焦存储领域
entry.content:
快科技10月21日消息，华为宣布第七届奥林帕斯奖正式启动全球征集，聚焦Agentic AI数据基础设施两大方向四道难题，设置2个奥林帕斯奖和5个奥林帕斯先锋奖。

奥林帕斯奖由华为于2019年设立，旨在鼓励全球科研工作者投入数据存储领域基础理论研究，已成为数据存储领域具有影响力的专业奖项之一。

随着AI技术从传统应用向Agent智能应用演进，数据不仅在规模上持续增长，留存、管理与应用方式也在发生改变。

因此本届聚焦解决Agentic AI数据基础设施中存储介质成本高、推理能效比低、数据供给不精准、知识泛化和演进难等问题。

其中方向一围绕每bit极致性价比的存储技术，下设两道难题。难题一是海量数据的超高密度存储与高效检索，难题二是状态数据的内存型存储介质与近存加速技术。

方向二聚焦Agentic AI原生的数据底座。难题三是以Token生产效率为中心的高效数据供给技术，难题四则基于本体知识图谱的高泛化、可演进知识表征技术。

评选从技术价值和商业价值两个维度综合评判，涵盖目标达成度、技术创新性、技术成熟度、可应用性、可扩展性和经济效益。

申报时间为2026年10月20日至2027年3月31日，成果评审在2027年4月至7月，颁奖典礼定于2027年8月。

entry.title: The Bridge to Agent-Scale Git Infrastructure
entry.content:
Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip.

In an earlier blog post, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture:

  • Minimize coordination
  • Decouple storage from compute

In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own.

How we got here

The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly.

While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived.

Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady.

During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process:

No repository left behind

So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories?

In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push.

This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently.

So, we’re changing the scope of the quorum from the whole repository to individual references.

Holding a repository-wide lock for the entire reference update, round trips included, turns the quorum into a single, unordered request queue with one write in flight at a time. Each write in that queue takes as long as the slowest healthy replica. As the write rate grows, so does the queue, and each write waits longer than the one before it.

With per-reference serialization, only writes that contend on a shared reference must wait for each other. In practice, most writes to a repository touch different references—for example, agents and developers pushing to their own branches—so they no longer wait on each other. Each write still experiences the cross-region latency but writes to different references can be in flight at the same time. That removes the single bottleneck on the repository. We can visualize how queueing and timeouts build up by comparing the two approaches side by side under similar load:

These changes raise a repository’s write throughput ceiling roughly in proportion to how many references are being written at once, and get the last remaining repositories into Azure. In internal testing with realistic traffic, writes to different references consistently saw 3–4x higher throughput at lower latency.

Scaling reads on their own

Most repositories are heavily read-skewed, with somewhere between 100 and 1,000 reads for every write. Today, reads and writes hit the same replicas, so they compete for the same resources and can’t be scaled independently.

Decoupling storage from compute changes that. Once repository data is durably stored in Azure Blob Storage and updated with each incoming write, we can begin to decouple read traffic from the write quorum, and independently scale the compute needed for each. For example, reads would benefit from far more in-memory cache than we give them today, but that memory is also needed for compaction. Once they’re separated, each gets its own configuration.

The first step is making object storage a member of the quorum, but a special one that we call a virtual replica. The compute that represents it is our first fully ephemeral node. It serves as a bridge to object storage, streaming incoming writes and serving no reads. Because it’s a member of the quorum, a write isn’t acknowledged until it’s durable in object storage.

That adds a little latency to each write, but just like the cross-region round trip, per-reference serialization keeps it from becoming a throughput bottleneck. The virtual write replica also coalesces transactions on disjoint references into a single set of network I/Os to object storage, so a busy repository pays for one round trip across many concurrent writes instead of one per write. For now, the virtual write replica also handles compaction, and read replicas inherit the compacted state.

With the virtual write replica in place, we can scale out as many virtual read replicas as a repository needs, on demand. Each read replica warms its cache from Azure Blob Storage and starts taking read traffic without joining the quorum, using object storage as the source of truth and reconciling its local state against it in the background.

This step unlocks significant read scale. In internal testing, our distributed load testing harness routinely found ceilings in the current architecture. Against virtual read replicas, the harness hit its own limits first. It also comes with a few challenges that are solved in subsequent steps:

  1. Virtual read replicas start out reconciling with object storage in the background, which makes them a good fit for some read workloads but not all of them. Serving every kind of read requires moving that reconciliation in-line, fetching only the reference state and data that changed since the replica last caught up.
  2. While we’ve incrementally increased write throughput by shifting to a per-reference model, the quorum remains the bounding factor for increasing further.

How can we push write throughput further?

What comes next

The GitHub of today was built on the Spokes quorum, and over the years Spokes has become much more than a quorum coordinator. It’s also an intelligent routing and load balancing layer, a unified API that internal clients use to access and transact repository data at well over 100 billion operations per day, and a collection of background systems we call “sweepers” that handle repository placement, repair, and rebalancing between storage nodes.

The vast majority of what lives under the Spokes service umbrella applies just as well to the new architecture as it does to the existing one. But we also recognize that the commit protocol that has taken GitHub to a billion repositories won’t take it to the next billion and beyond.

We’re not done yet. With these steps in place, the next limit is write throughput. Every write still waits on replicas that each hold a full copy of the repository, yet very little of a write actually needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, so they can be stored without anyone agreeing on them. What’s left is small, and the hard part is ordering it as fast as possible without moving the bottleneck somewhere else. Designing for that on a whiteboard is one thing. Doing it underneath a billion repositories that developers and agents are writing to around the clock is another. Getting there forced us to rethink the second-order effects too, like where durable reference state lives and how compaction and garbage collection scale.

Agent traffic isn’t slowing down, and each of these steps gives repositories more headroom as it lands, without waiting for the end state.

Coming next week: At GitHub Universe and in the final post in this series, we’ll take a tour through that end state, what it does for write throughput, the second-order problems we had to solve to get there, and why there’s still a (small) consensus group somewhere in the stack.

Thanks to Brian Celenza for their contributions to this post.

The post The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructurehttps://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/the-bridge-to-agent-scale-git-infrastructure/

entry.title: 8 eMudhra Certificates Are Compromised. Here's What You Need to Know
entry.content:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should do

Developer guidance

For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline

The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to knowhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/emudhra-certificate-compromise/

entry.title: Introducing Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust
entry.content:
Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain.

Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.

To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.

The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.

Performance and memory improvements

Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers:

As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and we’re hoping to find more.

You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration.

By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:

Try tsrs

TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm:

npm install tsrsnpx tsrs

Why now?

We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.

However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.

Why Rust?

You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?”

However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.

Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before.

This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.

How will the tsrs port be maintained?

First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post:

Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix.

We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.

Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.

What’s next?

Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.

Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rusthttps://blog.cloudflare.com/typescript-rust-port/

entry.title: How 3 Java Champions Are Using GitHub Copilot for Increased Productivity
entry.content:
AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.

Here are the tips they shared with us.

Meet the Java Champions

  • Vlad Mihalcea, founder of Hypersistence and author of the book High-Performance Java Persistence
  • Patrick Baumgartner, software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience
  • Frank Delporte, senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience

Vlad Mihalcea

GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.

For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.

What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?

I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.

It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.

I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.

Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?

I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.

This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.

Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.

One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.

Patrick Baumgartner

GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner

Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?

A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.

Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering.

The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner.

And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that.

Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently?

There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot.

Let’s start with the first one.

One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom.

Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work.

With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details.

The really important part was verification.

We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs.

That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence.

The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed.

For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result.

Can you share the second example?

A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell.

And then a real user did.

They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it.

We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged.

During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical.

That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution. It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent.

How about the third example?

The third example is completely different again.

Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app?

It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns.

Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary.

So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English.

It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition.

I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages.

What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product.

That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building.

How do you typically use Copilot?

I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore.

My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows.

I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go.

For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need.

I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction.

By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked.

That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed.

I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro.

But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me.

The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed.

Context is king.

Can you share some tips and best practices?

The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting.

For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit.

A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper.

I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful.

The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate.

Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work?

The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates.

“Done” should not mean that the model says it is done.

For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness.

The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done.

I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts.

The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills.

I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill.

The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there.

One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit, inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards.

The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain.

I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts.

The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model.

I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate:

change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again.

It continues until there are no findings left.

That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter.

I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly.

More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process.

That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck.

But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential.

How do you think AI is changing our profession?

I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another.

The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented.

So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution.

In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering.

And I like that.

Frank Delporte

GitHub profile: @FDelporte

How did you get started in tech?

I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-).

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports.

One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected. Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button.

This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer.

So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect.

Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.”

What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail:

I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi?

Check the pull request for the full conversation. Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation.

Can you share some tips and best practices?

  • Tell it where to look: For the Pi4J issue #622, I added two file paths. That is a tiny bit of effort that removes a huge amount of searching in a large codebase. You usually have a hunch about the neighbourhood even when you have no idea about the bug. Give it to the tool so it doesn’t need to investigate the complete code.
  • Ask for proof and tests: “Add a unit test to validate the change” is something I ask a lot these days. Well, asked, because it has now become a rule in my instructions file. It also prevents cases where the diagnosis was wrong, because the test won’t fail on the old code.
  • Ask why: If you don’t understand a fix, say so and ask. The explanation is a deliverable too and should be added into your project documentation or inside the ticket or pull request. It teaches everyone who reads the info later. For example, this also triggered more questions within the Pi4J team about virtual thread pinning on native calls.
  • Stay in control: All of these pull requests in Pi4J were reviewed and approved by maintainers before they went in. That’s the model that works best in this project: the agent does the investigation, the humans stay responsible for what ships. But also for my other projects I always do a review of the code that was generated by the tool. I always want to keep code readable and maintainable. Too often, a tool creates duplicate methods or recreates something which is already available in another place and should be combined. That’s your responsibility. You can go very fast these days with AI-assisted coding, which also means you can very fast create a mess. Don’t do that, keep your code manageable, your colleagues and future-self will thank you if they have to investigate bugs or make improvements later.

Get started with GitHub Copilot >

The post How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivityhttps://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-3-java-champions-are-using-github-copilot-for-increased-productivity/

entry.title: 引望携手宁德时代、时代电服共建智能换电生态 乾崑智驾补齐无感补能闭环
entry.content:
引望智能技术有限公司（引望）、宁德时代新能源科技股份有限公司（宁德时代）、时代电服科技有限公司今日在福建宁德正式签署《智能化补能生态战略合作协议》，三方将围绕新能源汽车智能换电生态开展全面战略合作，依托华为乾崑智驾与宁德时代巧克力换电网络深度打通，打造面向自动驾驶时代的 “无感补能” 全新体验，完善乾崑智驾智能充换电完整生态。

　　宁德时代董事长兼 CEO 曾毓群，华为高级副总裁、引望公司 CEO 靳玉志，宁德时代市场体系联席总裁杨峻等领导出席本次签约仪式。

　　根据协议，三方将强化换电电池、换电网络层面的协同合作，联合行业生态伙伴共建一体化智能换电体系。本次合作核心是实现乾崑智驾与巧克力换电网络底层生态互联，系统级打通车端、站端、云端的数据与服务链路。依托电池实时状态、用户出行大数据的智能预判与主动调度，搭载乾崑方案的车辆可自主识别补能需求、自主寻找换电站、自主入库、自动对位，完成99 秒全自动换电后自主驶离，实现全流程无人干预的智能补能闭环。

　　这意味着，搭载华为乾崑智能汽车解决方案的车型，未来将新增智能化换电选项，补能不再局限于充电桩，形成 “充电 + 换电” 双轨并行的完整智能补能体系。

　　此前，引望于 2025 年底推出 “10 分钟乾崑智驾生活圈”，将高阶辅助驾驶与停车缴费、智能充电、智能养车等高频用车场景深度融合。截至目前，便捷停车缴费已覆盖超 30 万个停车场，智能充电接入 200 万个充电桩场站，智能养车服务覆盖超 3000 家洗车门店。本次接入宁德时代巧克力换电网络，将进一步拓宽乾崑智驾生活圈边界，丰富自动驾驶时代的车生活场景。

　　三方表示，将坚持 “平等互利、资源共享、优势互补、发展共赢” 的合作原则，持续深化长期战略协同，联合构建体系化补能生态圈。依托各自在智能驾驶、动力电池、换电运营领域的核心能力，推动智能换电规模化落地，降低用户补能负担，让行车更安全、用车更便捷，助力新能源汽车产业智能化升级。
