entry.title: Cutting Our Inference Bill by 68% by Being Obsessive About Optimization
entry.content:
When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave.

Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before.

About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in.

How a review doubled in cost

The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data.

The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though.

At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models.

Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself.

The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost.

What else has changed since our last post?

One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!

So, where were the tokens going?

Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%,  cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that  most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.

That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.

It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.

That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.

Sharing a cached prefix between every repository

Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.

The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.

The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.

On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.

The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.

Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.

Fewer calls, fewer dollars

The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.

Change

What was happening

Effect of change

Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use

Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.

One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request

Reading files in parallel

In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.

Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB

Skipping reviewers on re-reviews

About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.

On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%.

Stopping after the review is posted

OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw.

About $0.07 saved per job

Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider

A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit.

Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none

Canceling canceled jobs

GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished.

Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled

The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it.

A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer.

Changing models and effort

The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked.

When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving.

Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment.

The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings.

Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%.

The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5.

On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below.

To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that.

Latency

We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers.

The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30.

By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been.

Review quality

A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened.

With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions.

First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence.

Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews.

Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low.

Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical.

So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next.

Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems.

Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%.

Where this leaves us

An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside.

Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for.

If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimizationhttps://blog.cloudflare.com/obsessive-inference-optimization/

entry.title: How to Continue a GitHub Copilot App Session in vs Code
entry.content:
The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.

In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to:

  • Open a Copilot app session in VS Code.
  • Review the agent’s changes line by line.
  • Continue the same conversation from your editor.
  • Modify and test the code locally.
  • Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session.

Prerequisites 

Before you begin, make sure you have: 

  • The GitHub Copilot app installed and signed in. 
  • Visual Studio Code installed and connected to the same GitHub account. 
  • A Copilot app session with code changes you want to review or continue. 
  • Permission to work in and push changes to the session’s repository. 

This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests.

1. Start with a session in the Copilot app

Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.

A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.

You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.

2. Open the session in VS Code

From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.

VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.

That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:

  • The session context: The task, plan, and conversation remain available.
  • The diff: The files and lines changed by the agent are ready for review.
  • The worktree: VS Code opens the same isolated working tree the session used.

You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.

3. Review the agent’s changes

Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.

Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:

  • The code solves the requested problem.
  • The implementation follows the repository’s conventions.
  • Error states and edge cases are handled appropriately.
  • Tests cover the behavior that changed.
  • No unrelated files or behaviors were modified.

The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:

Explain why you changed this function instead of adding a new helper. Identify any behavior this could affect.

You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.

4. Make a hands-on edit

Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.

This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:

  • Refining a label or error message.
  • Renaming a variable for clarity.
  • Adjusting layout or styling.
  • Adding a missing test case.
  • Applying a repository-specific convention.

You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch.

5. Run and verify the project locally

Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include:

  • npm install
  • npm test
  • npm run lint
  • npm run dev

Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself.

If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor.

For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work.

6. Continue with Copilot or keep editing yourself

At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step:

  • Prompt Copilot when the change requires repository-wide analysis or repetitive edits.
  • Edit directly when you know the exact change you want.
  • Use both approaches iteratively as you test and refine the implementation.

For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot:

Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components.

Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.”

7. Commit and push the finished changes

When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal:

  • git status
  • git add
  • git commit -m "Refine session changes"
  • git push

Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work.

There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually.

A continuous workflow from agent to editor

Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish.

The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow.

Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding.

The post How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Codehttps://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-to-continue-a-github-copilot-app-session-in-vs-code/

entry.title: 赛力斯康波：问界2027年进入欧洲市场并拓展全球
entry.content:
快科技10月15日消息，赛力斯集团董事、副总裁康波在2026巴黎车展现场接受央视财经频道采访时表示，问界计划于2027年秋季正式进入欧洲市场，并逐步拓展全球市场。目前问界正积极推进监管合规认证与本地化运营，欧洲版车型同步推进中。

据悉，问界汽车的WVTA欧盟整车型式认证工作已全面启动。

此次巴黎车展上，问界以“智慧重塑豪华”为主题，携问界M9、M8、M7、M6四款车型以及魔方技术平台亮相。问界M9在50万元以上市场已累计21个月保持销量领先，问界M8在40万元级别市场连续6个月销量第一，问界M7累计交付量已突破40万辆。2026年1月15日，问界第一百万辆整车下线，从品牌成立到百万辆达成仅用时不到三年。

问界进军欧洲并非孤例。2026年以来，中国新能源品牌出海欧洲步伐明显加快。中国品牌在欧洲市场份额第二季度已接近11%，比亚迪、吉利、零跑、奇瑞等品牌增速显著。

entry.title: 商务部部长王文涛会见美国苹果公司执行董事长蒂姆·库克
entry.content:
快科技10月15日消息，据商务部官网公告，今日，商务部部长王文涛会见苹果公司执行董事长蒂姆·库克。双方就中美经贸关系、人工智能发展、苹果公司在华业务等议题进行交流。

王文涛表示，在两国元首构建“基于尊重、公平、对等的中美建设性战略稳定关系”的共识引领下，中美经贸磋商取得积极成果。

中方倡导人工智能发展安全可控、普惠向善、治理合作。希望苹果公司发挥沟通桥梁作用，为推动中美经贸关系持续稳定向好发展贡献力量。

当前，中国坚定不移扩大高水平对外开放，持续优化营商环境，消费市场扩容升级，绿色供应链不断壮大，将为跨国企业在华投资向智能、绿色、创新转型提供更广阔空间。

希望苹果公司继续深耕中国市场，共享中国式现代化发展机遇。

库克表示，苹果公司看好中国发展前景，将进一步扩大在华业务，并愿为推动美中经贸关系稳定健康发展发挥积极作用。

此次会面是库克本次中国之行的收官重要政企沟通环节，也是他9月卸任苹果CEO、转任执行董事长后的首次访华，行程覆盖广州、北京两地，贯穿产业交流、政企会晤、生态合作多个维度。

entry.title: Staying Evergreen: How We Automated Secure Access and Repo Hygiene in a Shared Org
entry.content:
Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose.

To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer.

We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen, a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization.

Meet Evergreen

Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows:

  1. Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed.
  2. Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived.

Two design principles shaped everything:

Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome.

Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written into the repo’s tracking issue, so reverting a mistake is as easy as a copy-paste to Copilot.

How it works: One brain, many hands

Under the hood, Evergreen is a small Go webhook server running in a container. But the interesting part is the choreography. Every moving piece is a stock GitHub feature: a GitHub App, scheduled actions, webhooks, issues, custom properties, and plain files in a repo. Nothing exotic to reinvent.

A controller that keeps time

A dedicated controller repo acts as Evergreen’s clock and its memory. Four scheduled GitHub Actions workflows fire repository_dispatch events on a quarterly cadence, and the app wakes up and does the work:

Reviews open two weeks before their cleanup runs, and there’s a hard grace period baked in so a stray manual run can never fast‑forward the guillotine. Each workflow also supports workflow_dispatch, so we can trigger any step by hand as needed.

State you can git blame

Evergreen tracks every repo’s status as a JSON file (one per repository) committed to the controller repo under state/repos/<repo_id>.json. The snapshot of who had access, when the review opened, the deadline, who decided, and what happened all lives there. Here’s a completed review where a Hubber kept Alice’s access and let Bob’s lapse:

{  "repo_id": 123456789,  "full_name": "the-org/acme-trial",  "last_seen_at": "2026-04-13T00:05:00Z",  "access_review": {    "deadline": "2026-04-27T00:00:00Z",    "status": "renewed",    "collaborators_at_open": [      { "login": "alice", "name": "Alice Example", "permission": "admin" },      { "login": "bob", "name": "Bob Example", "permission": "write" }    ],    "renewed_logins": ["alice"],    "decided_by": "carol-hubber",    "decided_at": "2026-04-15T16:42:10Z",    "tracking_issue": { "repo_id": 123456789, "number": 42 }  },  "staleness": {    "last_activity_at": "2026-04-15T16:42:10Z",    "warned_at": null,    "archive_deadline": null,    "status": "active",    "tracking_issue": null  }}

The best part: because state is just files in git, the commit history is the audit trail. Want to know why someone lost access last spring? git log the state file. There’s no separate database or bespoke audit pipeline to track.

Issue‑ops, everywhere it matters

Evergreen does its talking through issues inside each repository. When an access review kicks off, every repo gets a checklist issue:

The interaction model is delightfully simple: check the boxes for who stays, then close the issue. That’s it. When the issue closes, Evergreen listens for the issues.closed webhook event, reads the checkboxes, retains the checked collaborators, and revokes the rest, then posts a receipt comment listing exactly what it kept and what it removed.

Only the right humans can pull the lever

Closing an access review issue is a privileged action, so Evergreen guards it. If someone who isn’t a Hubber closes an issue, the app quietly reopens it and posts a note explaining why. Decisions only count when they come from the people authorized to make them.

Informing the right people

Here’s a subtle problem: we know the people who need to respond to a review are Hubbers, but we didn’t always know which Hubber(s) owned a given repository.

Evergreen resolves the right people to notify through a fallback chain:

  1. If a repo sets an evergreen_repo_owner custom property (a @user or @org/team), use it.
  2. Otherwise, look at recent issue and commit authors and cc the ones who are on the access review team, i.e., the Hubbers actually working in that repo.

The result: the right owners get pinged automatically, without anyone maintaining a spreadsheet of “who owns what.”

Fail secure, and fail closed

When a review deadline passes with no response, cleanup revokes every collaborator in the snapshot. We were careful about a subtle edge case: what if some removals succeed while others hit a transient API error? Marking the review “done” while a removal is still outstanding would be a quiet inconsistency, and we didn’t want that.

So Evergreen fails closed. If any removal fails, the review stays pending and the issue stays open, and the next run retries the stragglers. It only records “revoked” once every removal actually succeeded. And whatever gets removed is written into the issue, so restoring access is a matter of re‑adding the handles it listed.

The user experience: automation that feels considerate

Automated housekeeping has a reputation for being the office smoke alarm: loud, easy to ignore, and usually going off while you’re cooking something perfectly fine. We worked hard to make Evergreen feel like the opposite:

  • It comes to you. The work happens as an issue in your repo.
  • It tags the right people. No “who owns this?” archaeology.
  • It’s crystal clear about the ask. Every issue states what to do, the exact deadline, and precisely what happens if you ignore it.
  • It nudges before it acts. A reminder comment lands before the deadline: no surprise revocations.
  • It has an escape hatch. Org owners (Hubbers) can opt out by setting a custom property (evergreen_exempt_from_access_review or evergreen_exempt_from_archive).

Rolling it out carefully

Automation that manages access and archives repositories deserves a careful rollout, especially into a large, active org (ours has 1,400+ Hubbers, and many more customers and partners). We wanted the very first run to be a complete non‑event. A few practices got us there:

Dry‑run first. Evergreen ships with a DRY_RUN mode that logs every write it would make without touching a single collaborator or repo. We ran it against the real org and read the logs like tea leaves until we trusted the decisions it wanted to make.

Overcommunicate. Before flipping the switch, we broadcast what was coming, when, and what people needed to do, so the first issue anyone saw wasn’t a surprise. We found that when you’re telling a large group the same thing for the seventh time, it’s often when many are still hearing it for the first time.

Watch everything with Splunk. Evergreen emits structured logfmt logs to a dedicated Splunk index. That observability is how we caught edge cases in the wild (empty collaborator lists, unusual permissions, repos with issues disabled) and tightened the logic before they mattered.

Respect the platform’s speed limits. When you open issues and post comments across every repo in a big org, you slam into GitHub’s secondary rate limits for content creation: 80 requests/minute and 500/hour. While this is a thoughtful preventative control to avoid system abuse, it requires a bit of intention when automating IssueOps at large scale.

So Evergreen paces itself by construction. It processes repos in batches, spaces out each content‑creating call by a couple of seconds, and sleeps between batches to let the rolling window clear, and it only counts the repos that actually create content, so a quiet quarter where nothing’s eligible still runs fast. We opted for proactive avoidance over reactive back‑off.

Lessons we’re taking with us

  • Make the safe path the default path. Fail secure, then make responding easy enough that failing secure rarely triggers.
  • Use the primitives you already have. Issues, webhooks, custom properties, and git history did the work of a bespoke UI, a job queue, and an audit database.
  • Meet people where they work. An issue in your repo beats a dashboard you’ll never open.
  • Logs are a revert button. Writing every change into the issue turned “oops” into “paste these three handles into a Copilot session.”
  • Respect the limits. At org scale, rate limits aren’t an edge case: they’re the design constraint.

Keep your org evergreen

Routine hygiene is the kind of work that’s easy to defer and perfect to automate. The trick isn’t heroic cleanup sprints: it’s making the boring, safe thing happen on a schedule, with a friendly face and an undo button.

That’s Evergreen. And because it’s built entirely from native GitHub features, you can stand up the same pattern yourself.

Ready to make repository hygiene routine? Start with one recurring access or archival task, then use GitHub Apps, actions, issues, and custom properties to automate the problem away.

entry.title: The Next Developer Interface Is Ambient Intelligence
entry.content:
For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine.

AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls.

We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different.

AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like.

This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem.

That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated.

So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence.

That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath.

I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control.

Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context.

Why physical controls are interesting again

I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces.

Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working.

The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control.

Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back.

GUIs made software visual. Mouse made navigation easier. The web made it connected. Mobile made touch natural. Agents add intent and action. The interface now includes ambient control.

The interface moves into the background

That is why GitHub worked with Logitech to integrate the GitHub Copilot app directly into the experience. Developers can run agentic workflows in control, map a repeated prompt, start or resume a session, and decide through real use whether a physical control helps you stay in flow.

This is still early, so the important questions are engineering questions. How much repository and organizational context should an agent retain? Which tool calls can run automatically? How should credentials, network access, and secrets be scoped? What evidence should accompany a change? How do multiple agents coordinate without duplicating work or creating conflicting pull requests? Products such as MX Keypad let us explore one practical part of that system: how developers invoke, steer, and resume agentic work without losing focus.

For decades, developers learned to speak computer: syntax, commands, APIs, shortcuts, and the occasional incantation copied from a seven-year-old issue comment. Now computers are getting better at meeting us halfway. The best interface will not have the most panels or AI buttons. It will understand enough context, preserve meaningful control, and get out of the way so we can build software that matters.

The goal is not to remove developers from the work. It is to remove friction around the work. Pairing MX Keypad with GitHub Copilot Pro+ gives developers a concrete experiment: choose one repeated interruption, map it to a control, and see whether it preserves focus.

If you want to try it, you can do so here and get three months of GitHub Copilot Pro+.

The post The next developer interface is ambient intelligence appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

entry.title: 新凯来半导体设备全面量产！万里眼90GHz示波器卖爆了：国产替代加速
entry.content:
快科技10月14日消息，2026湾区半导体产业生态博览会今日在深圳开幕。新凯来一名工作人员对媒体表示，公司半导体设备已实现量产，目前国内很多晶圆厂已经在用，应用覆盖先进逻辑和存储领域。

新凯来此次展示了覆盖半导体制造关键环节的装备矩阵。 展品涵盖刻蚀、扩散、薄膜沉积、光学检测、光学量测、物理与X射线量测等设备，覆盖工艺装备和量检测装备两大方向。其中新增公开了PMI图形掩模缺陷检测设备和mEBI多电子束晶圆缺陷检测设备两款新品。

据华尔街投行伯恩斯坦2026年5月发布的报告，2025年中国本土厂商在国内晶圆制造设备市场的份额已从2024年的16%提升至21%。

其中刻蚀设备和薄膜沉积设备的本土份额分别达到31%和27%，但量检测环节仅约10%。新凯来半导体设备的量产落地，正是国产设备从单点突破走向全流程覆盖的关键一步。

新凯来旗下万里眼带来的90GHz超高速实时示波器成为本届展会焦点。 万里眼工作人员透露，该产品目前需求旺盛，已进入多家国内头部客户的研发测试环节，产能有点跟不上。

这款示波器带宽达90GHz，位居全球第二，打破了西方国家对中国60GHz以上实时示波器的出口管制。它采用全新慧眼架构，采样率高达每秒2000亿次，存储深度达40亿样点，能够精准捕获并分析纳米芯片的瞬态信号。

万里眼CEO刘桑此前透露，产品已实现商用，下单后5至8周可交付，已在华为等多家企业和科研单位应用。

新凯来子公司启云方的EDA软件同样在加速落地。 启云方去年发布了原理图和PCB设计软件，性能较行业标杆提升约30%，可将硬件开发周期缩短40%。

entry.title: 全栈国产化！2874.9万元大单落地：银河麒麟、南大通用、H3C、华为等中标
entry.content:
快科技10月14日消息，据中国政府采购网公告，天津市疾病预防控制中心现代化疾病预防控制体系信息化建设项目中标结果近日公布。项目总预算2900万元，分两包采购，中标总金额达2874.9万元。

第1包由天津市天河计算机技术有限公司中标，金额51.9万元。采购内容为基础软件产品，包括银河麒麟桌面操作系统200套、服务器操作系统20套，南大通用安全数据库管理系统GBase 8s V8.8共4套、多模多态数据库管理系统GBase 8c V6共1套。该包评审得分高达100分。

第2包由中电云脑（天津）科技有限公司中标，金额2823万元，是本次采购的硬件大头。品牌涵盖H3C、华为、浪潮等主流国产厂商。核心设备包括H3C S6850-56HF-G存储交换机、华为OceanStor系列存储设备、浪潮NF5280M6服务器等，同时包含中电云脑定制开发服务。

值得关注的是，第2包明确采购智算一体机2套和通算一体机1套。这标志着疾控信息化正从传统通用算力向AI智算算力延伸，为传染病监测预警、流行病学建模等场景提供算力底座。该项目明确不接受进口产品，实现全栈国产化。

从采购规模看，2874.9万元是今年以来疾控系统信创信息化建设中金额较大的项目之一。银河麒麟、南大通用、H3C、华为、浪潮等国产厂商的集体中标，反映出信创基础设施在公共卫生领域的加速渗透。

entry.title: Stellantis CEO明确：不会出售玛莎拉蒂品牌
entry.content:
快科技10月14日消息，巴黎车展期间，Stellantis集团首席执行官安东尼奥·菲洛萨接受媒体采访，针对市场持续流传的玛莎拉蒂出售传闻作出明确表态：集团没有出售玛莎拉蒂的计划，传闻绝非事实，玛莎拉蒂将继续作为集团旗下唯一豪华品牌长期运营。

近期市场之所以传出出售猜测，源于玛莎拉蒂经营承压，销量持续下滑，电气化转型投入巨大，盈利表现不佳。

Stellantis此前调整业务架构，不再将玛莎拉蒂作为独立业务板块单独财报核算，改由区域统筹管理，这一调整进一步引发投资者猜测，认为集团可能剥离该品牌回笼资金。

菲洛萨强调，玛莎拉蒂拥有百年品牌底蕴与独特的豪华跑车基因，在整个Stellantis品牌矩阵里具备不可替代的战略价值。

集团将继续推进玛莎拉蒂Folgore纯电电气化转型计划，现有产品GranTurismo、GranCabrio、Grecale均已推出纯电版本，后续Quattroporte总裁、Levante莱凡特的换代车型也在研发规划之中。

不过集团会优化资本分配策略，把更多资源倾斜给Jeep、Ram、标致、菲亚特等规模更大、盈利性更强的核心品牌；玛莎拉蒂则依托集团共享的整车、电控技术平台，控制研发成本，提升经营效率。

豪华品牌培育周期漫长，出售玛莎拉蒂不仅很难拿到预期估值，也会直接丢掉集团高端市场的卡位，虽然保留品牌，但玛莎拉蒂未来会缩减非必要投入，聚焦高端性能车型。

值得注意的是，据行业多方信源爆料，Stellantis、华为、江淮三方合作接近落地，目前规划两款全新纯电车型，整车由合肥尊界超级工厂负责制造。

两款新车分别为中大型纯电SUV、大型纯电GT，定位高端豪华电动车型，玛莎拉蒂方面希望先上纯电GT，SUV后续跟上，国内版本归属尊界品牌销售，海外市场则悬挂玛莎拉蒂三叉戟标识。

【本文结束】如需转载请务必注明出处：快科技

entry.title: GitHub Availability Report: September 2026
entry.content:
Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months.

The short version of August and September: we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete.

By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added.

We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. We disabled that process during planned handoffs while improving recovery.

Outside the regional migration, 24 authentication-core tables moved off GitHub’s oldest shared database, removing approximately one million queries per second from its replicas. The database cluster supporting issues and pull requests removed approximately 980 million unnecessary edit-history rows, creating an estimated 1.8 terabytes of recoverable storage. Weekly deadlocks fell approximately 77% from their June peak, and continuous cleanup now prevents the same unbounded growth from returning.

Half of sampled pull request traffic can now continue with limited functionality when a shared dependency fails. Production results showed several read operations remained available during a shared-database incident. Database traffic routing can also add capacity automatically during spikes; one group expanded from 14 to 19 instances during a September 23 increase in pull request activity. A production overload control now lets responders protect higher-priority API and web workflows by rejecting lower-priority requests before broader saturation. Operator documentation and training are complete.

GitHub Actions also gained operating headroom. Production changes reduced measured Redis operations by approximately 28% and relative CPU by approximately 30%. A separate infrastructure cache reduced Redis bandwidth by 84%, average response time by 66%, median response time for the primary inventory request by 96%, and queued requests by 95%.

The August 6 actions outage, August 17 github.com outage, September failover disruption, and controlled capacity pause are reminders that measured improvements matter only when they reduce customer risk under real conditions. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

September 13 09:16 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 28 minutes)

What happened?

Impact summary

Duration: approximately 2 hours

Customers may have seen requests fail, run slowly, or remain pending when opening or updating issues and pull requests, calling APIs, creating access tokens, starting GitHub Actions workflows, or signing up.

~96% of the customer requests creating issues through the web interface were impacted during the incident window. In addition, 90% of new customer signup and ~4% of actions workflows also experienced intermittent failures.

What went wrong and why?

A background data-cleanup job increased load on a shared database. The job had a safeguard designed to slow its writes when database replicas fell behind, but the safeguard did not account for incoming load on the primary database server. As a result, the job continued running until the primary reached its connections limit. When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that depended on it could not complete reliably.

Two other factors increased the impact and delayed recovery. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept resending writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover.

How did we respond?

  1. A background data-cleanup job began writing to a shared database.
  2. The job’s safeguard monitored replica lag but did not account for load building on the database’s primary server.
  3. The primary ran out of available connections, causing requests across dependent services to fail or run slowly.
  4. Automated monitoring detected the incident, and we traced the failures to load on the shared database.
  5. We reduced internal load and paused the background job.
  6. The database recovered, and error rates across the affected services returned to normal.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We are implementing additional safeguards to improve database resilience and service availability. These measures will better control background processing based on available database capacity, reduce unnecessary retries during failures, and limit the impact of slow database requests.
  • We are also improving service startup behavior to ensure that temporary database connectivity issues do not unnecessarily affect service recovery.

September 28 21:16 UTC (lasting 52 minutes) 

What happened?

Impact summary 

Duration: approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes 

This incident impacted Copilot code review across github.com and GHEC data-residency regions. Affected customers saw Copilot remain in a reviewing state without a review appearing, with delays ranging from ~30 minutes to a max of 2 hours. 

Some reviews on github.com continued to complete normally during the incident, while reviews in data-residency regions did not. Some customers still received delayed error messages for requests made during the incident. 

What went wrong and why?

Copilot code review uses a separate service to run reviews and 2 versions of the results are returned: a limited copy that excludes the review comments and a full copy that includes the completed review. Copilot code review posts reviews only from the full copy. A change to that service began sending the full copy only for some customers. For other customers, only the limited copy was sent.

As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully. The missing review results were not detected due to lack of monitoring. The incident was detected as some of the reviews remained incomplete for more than 30 minutes, triggering an alert to first responders.

We mitigated the incident by reverting the change.

How did we respond?

  1. A change to the service that runs Copilot code reviews began rolling out, and review results stopped appearing on pull requests. The change reached every environment.
  2. Reviews began timing out, triggering an alert to the Copilot code review team. We declared an incident.
  3. We traced the failures to the change and began reverting it.
  4. While the revert completed its required checks, we posted the incident on the GitHub Status page.
  5. The revert then reached all the affected regions. We resolved the incident and advised customers to request affected reviews again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

  • We are strengthening the reliability of Copilot code reviews by adding safeguards throughout the review and delivery process. These improvements will help ensure that completed reviews are delivered successfully, allow failed reviews to recover automatically, and provide earlier notification when issues occur.
  • We are also improving our monitoring and deployment processes so that problems can be identified and addressed more quickly.

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

The post GitHub availability report: September 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

entry.title: From 2,500 Requests to 24: Rebuilding Star History Without the Stargazers
entry.content:
Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away.

Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page.

The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper.

Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything.

What maintainers need from star history

We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators. After the access change, callers without the required permission could receive an empty response or a 403 Forbidden response.

That change also cut off tools that had used the old response to calculate star history, often without displaying or otherwise using the usernames it returned. So we talked with maintainers and tool builders to understand what they still needed. They used star history as an approximate signal of interest: to compare activity before and after a release, or to see whether an announcement reached new developers. What they cared about was the curve.

The old API response had made identity look like part of that contract because every timestamp arrived attached to a user. In practice, tools such as Star History needed counts and dates, not usernames or other user data. Once identity was no longer part of the requirement, we could design an aggregate endpoint for the actual job: retrieving changes in star counts over time at a useful resolution.

When the API change disrupted Star History, users rallied around the project. GitHub’s Community team listened and connected us with product engineering, who dug into our use case and worked alongside us to design a purpose-built endpoint. A difficult situation became a constructive collaboration between GitHub, Star History, and the broader community—ultimately leading to a better solution.

Tianzhou Chen, star-history.com maintainer and Bytebase co-founder

Why the original endpoint was expensive

Once we knew what maintainers needed, the next step was understanding why the original design couldn’t provide it cheaply. The original GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers endpoint was built to answer a simple question: who starred this repository? It returned a paginated list of people, and if the request specified a custom media type, each entry also included when the star was created.

The star model was built for the same job. It records the current set of people who have starred a repository, which keeps showing a star count or a list of stargazers simple. It was not designed as a historical event log: when someone removes a star, that record is removed. When tools began using the list as a time series, reconstructing a growth curve meant retrieving individual identities and processing every current star. Because each page held at most 100 people, the work grew with the repository’s popularity: building the full curve for react/react, with about 251,000 stars, took about 2,511 requests, so tools often ran into rate limits or sampled pages instead of reading them all.

Serving a page required the database to query the repository’s current stars. Due to a bug in the pagination implementation, every request also counted all of those stars to work out how many pages existed, even though the caller received only one page of up to 100 people. On a highly starred repository, that meant counting many thousands of entries on every request. In the week before we restricted access, nearly 37,000 of these count queries ran slowly enough to be logged, averaging nearly 3 seconds each, and database safeguards killed more than 1,000 of them, which contributed to request timeouts.

The chart below shows what all that counting cost. After we restricted access, the database served about 60% fewer stargazer requests, and the total time it spent on the count query fell by about 80%.

Approaches we considered

Removing identities handled the privacy requirement. The harder part was keeping each request from scanning the repository’s entire current star set.

Keeping events without identities

Our first spike kept one record per star and returned the starred_at value without the stargazer’s identity for callers who lacked collaborator access. At first, this looked like the quickest path forward, because it directly served the request we had heard from tool builders. It also closed the identity-harvesting path with a relatively small change to the existing serialization and authorization flow.

This approach addressed identity exposure and would have allowed existing tools to keep working. But API consumers would still have to paginate through and process potentially many thousands of individual records to build an aggregate history. It also tied the new use case to an endpoint and pagination model designed for listing people rather than retrieving trends.

Aggregating, then paginating

Aggregation seemed like the obvious next step. Instead of returning one row per star, the query could group stars into daily or weekly buckets, sort those buckets, and paginate the much smaller result.

The problem was where pagination happened. In a straightforward SQL query, the database first finds all stars for the repository, groups them into buckets, and sorts those buckets. Only then does it apply LIMIT, which controls how many buckets are returned, and OFFSET, which determines where the page begins:

all matching stars -> bucket every row by day or week -> sort every bucket -> OFFSET/LIMIT -> response

For a popular repository, an anonymous request could still scan and aggregate many thousands of index entries to return a handful of buckets. Returning fewer buckets would shrink the JSON response, but it would not reduce the expensive grouping and sorting the database had already performed. For react/react, reading the full history that way would have meant examining roughly 6 million rows, because every one of the 24 requests would have reprocessed all of its stars. To reduce the query cost, we had to narrow the rows before aggregation began.

Filtering by time before grouping

The design we shipped paginates star history by calendar week. For each request, it translates page and per_page into an indexed created_at range, filters the stars to those weeks, and then groups the matching records into daily counts. A response includes up to 30 weeks, and increasing page moves backward through the repository’s history.

indexed date range -> group rows in that range -> daily buckets -> response

With the date range applied first, each request processes the weeks being returned instead of every current star in the repository. For tools, that means one request now covers up to 30 weeks of history, no matter how many stars the repository has. For react/react, that’s about 24 requests instead of about 2,511, and the database examines each star about once (roughly 251,000 rows) across the full history. This fits the primary use case because maintainers usually inspect growth across weeks or around a known release, launch, or event. Week-based ranges also align with other repository activity APIs: the response follows the same shape as the weekly commit activity endpoint, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stats/commit_activity.

The time-range design limits each request to a defined period, but it does not limit the number of stars within that range. A week with an unusually large number of stars can therefore still produce a slow or expensive query. The normal request path no longer queries every current star, but exceptionally dense weeks remain a scaling limitation.

Comparing the performance of the old and new API paths also surfaced other places where GitHub was counting stars on demand. We found the same pattern on the repository stargazers page on GitHub.com and updated it to use the repository’s cached star count. Slow queries from that page, which had numbered in the hundreds each week, dropped to zero. We recently shipped a similar fix to other stargazer API endpoints.

The chart below shows slow and killed stargazer count queries each week, by where they came from.

What we learned

  1. A smaller response does not always mean a cheaper query. LIMIT and OFFSET reduced the number of results returned, but they did not reduce the grouping and sorting the database had already done. We had to look at the order in which the work happened.
  2. Start with what people are actually trying to do. Maintainers needed to compare trends. A list of identities was simply how the old endpoint happened to provide the underlying data.
  3. Return only what the use case needs. Anything more is data someone else can misuse. Once we understood the job, we could remove individual identities without taking away the information maintainers relied on.
  4. Be clear about the tradeoffs that remain. The new endpoint is safer and more predictable, but calendar boundaries, removed stars, and unusually dense weeks still affect what it can return. Those details are part of the API contract too.

Restricting the original endpoint addressed the immediate problem. Listening to maintainers gave us something better than what we started with: star history that’s easier to get, cheaper to serve, and safer for everyone who stars a project.

Get repository star history, then share feedback in the GitHub Community discussion.
